newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ compulsory pension scheme no threat - Birch.
newsitem.headline: NZ compulsory pension scheme no threat - Birch.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Wednesday the compulsory superannuation scheme, due to be put to public vote in a referendum in September, was no threat to the new coalition government.
"I certainly don't see it as a threat," Birch told Reuters Financial Television in Hong Kong.

In an interview monitored by Reuters in Wellington, Birch said the decision to go to a referendum was a compromise negotiated when the coalition was formed in December 1996 between the conservative National Party and the nationalist New Zealand First Party.
"The New Zealand First Party was very keen on compulsory savings, the National government not so convinced but willing to subject the issue to a referendum," Birch said.
He said the government was working to make sure it achieved the best possible design for the proposed retirement savings scheme.
"If we get that right, the outcome could well be positive if the voters say yes to a referendum."
Asked how he planned to deal with MPs who opposed the plan, Birch said MPs had the right to debate the issue.

"I guess it will be a pretty animated debate, but I expect that once they see the design of the savings schemes they will see it as being an innovative piece of policy consistent with the reforms we have developed over the last decade.
"I don't think there will be any difficulty, if the referendum gets a green light, to gain the numbers to carry the legislation through the house."
The coalition agreement allows government MPs to argue for or against the scheme before the vote, but binds them to support the implementation of the law if there is a positive result.

However, a group of government backbenchers on Tuesday threatened to vote against a compulsory superannuation scheme if there is a low voter turnout at the referendum, threatening the government's majority.

The exact design of the proposed scheme is yet to be finalised but will take into account New Zealand First's policy that would eventually see at least eight percent of income diverted into pension savings.
If approved it would come into force in July, 1998.
